message.content:
Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{100}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}.
\]

For a fixed \(j\), write \(k=tj+s\), where \(t\ge 0\) and \(1\le s\le j\). Then

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor 101t+\frac{101s}{j}\right\rfloor
=
101t+\left\lfloor \frac{101s}{j}\right\rfloor.
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}
=
\frac{\sum_{s=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101s/j\rfloor}}{1-2^{-101}}.
\]

Therefore

\[
S=\frac{A}{1-2^{-101}},
\]

where

\[
A=\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{s=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101s/j\rfloor}.
\]

Now count how many pairs \((j,s)\) give each possible value of \(q=\lfloor 101s/j\rfloor\).

Since \(1\le s\le j\le 100\), we have \(1\le q\le 101\).  
If \(s=j\), then \(q=101\), and this happens \(100\) times.

If \(s<j\), then

\[
\frac{101s}{j}\le \frac{101(j-1)}{j}=101-\frac{101}{j}<100,
\]

so \(q\le 99\). Thus the only possible values are

\[
q\in\{1,2,\dots,99,101\}.
\]

We claim that for each \(q=1,\dots,99\), there are exactly \(50\) pairs \((j,s)\) with \(\lfloor 101s/j\rfloor=q\).

To see this, fix \(q\in\{1,\dots,99\}\) and put \(a=q+1\), so \(2\le a\le 100\). Since \(101\) is prime and \(j\le 100\), equality cannot occur, so

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101s}{j}\right\rfloor=q
\iff
q<\frac{101s}{j}<a
\iff
qj<101s<aj.
\]

For a fixed \(j\), the interval for \(s\) has length \(j/101<1\), so there is at most one such \(s\). Let \(u\) be the least positive residue of \(aj\pmod{101}\). If such an \(s\) exists, then

\[
u=aj-101s
\]

satisfies \(1\le u<j\). Conversely, if \(1\le u<j\) and \(u\equiv aj\pmod{101}\), then

\[
s=\frac{aj-u}{101}
\]

is an integer satisfying the required inequality. Thus the number of pairs for this \(q\) is

\[
\#\{j\in\{1,\dots,100\}: u<j\}.
\]

Now pair \(j\) with \(101-j\). Since

\[
u(101-j)\equiv a(101-j)\equiv -aj\equiv 101-u(j)\pmod{101},
\]

we have

\[
u(j)<j \iff u(101-j)>101-j.
\]

Also \(u(j)=j\) is impossible, because that would imply \((a-1)j\equiv0\pmod{101}\), contradicting \(1\le j\le100\) and \(a\ne1\). Therefore exactly one member of each pair \(\{j,101-j\}\) works, and there are \(50\) such pairs. So indeed

\[
C_q=50 \qquad (1\le q\le 99),
\]

and

\[
C_{101}=100.
\]

Therefore

\[
A
=
50\sum_{q=1}^{99}2^{-q}+100\cdot 2^{-101}.
\]

Using \(\sum_{q=1}^{99}2^{-q}=1-2^{-99}\),

\[
A
=
50(1-2^{-99})+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=
50(1-2^{-100}).
\]

Finally,

\[
S
=
\frac{50(1-2^{-100})}{1-2^{-101}}
=
\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
